rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the discussion of Alif Lām Mīm was already given in Sūrah al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: Research on ّٓمTٓال has already been presented in Sūrah Baqarah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses of this sūrah resemble the opening of Sūrah al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: like the previous sūrah, the introductory verses of this sūrah as well resemble as those of Sūrah Baqarah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanzīl means revelation delivered gradually and elaborately, not merely revelation.
rows.anchor: the word لۡیِزۡنَت does not mean merely to reveal but to reveal gradually in an elaborate way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word al-kitāb refers to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: The word ِبٰتِکۡال refers to the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā rayba fīhi means there is no doubt that this Book was revealed by God; Islahi says this is the same sense he gave in al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: The words ِہۡیِ ف َبۡیَ ر َلَا express that there is no doubt in the fact that it has been revealed by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh and Jews disputed the Prophet’s claim that the Book came from God, accusing him of inventing it and falsely ascribing it to God.
rows.anchor: They would accuse the Prophet (sws) of concocting the Qur’ān and would assert that in order to force his ideas on them he

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question expresses amazement that opposition has made the deniers so blind and deaf that they call the revelation claim false; anyone with truthfulness and justice would not say this.
rows.anchor: This question expresses amazement: Have these people become so blind and deaf in opposing the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Qur’an the truth means the ancestral religion is baseless and the religion to which the Book invites them is true.
rows.anchor: the ancestral religion to which these people adhere is totally baseless and false; the true religion is the one this book is inviting them to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic answer also insists that the Book truly comes from God and warns that continued denial will bring consequences.
rows.anchor: these people should not think that this book is being falsely ascribed to God; it is, in fact, from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book’s purpose is to warn a people of their worldly and otherworldly fate so that they may be guided; this people is the Arabs, who had no prophet after Ishmael.
rows.anchor: the word م ۡوَقٌ refers to the Arabs to whom no prophet came after Ishmael (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation is a great favor to the unlettered Arabs, who should value and honor it.
rows.anchor: These words also express the great favour God has done to the unlettered Arabs by revealing this Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice is to judge a nation after sending a warner and, after a respite, destroy it if it does not reform.
rows.anchor: when the Almighty sends a warner to a nation, then the fate of that nation is judged.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book warns through two central beliefs: monotheism and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: There are two specific contents that constitute this warning: the beliefs of monotheism and hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The monotheistic warning rejects false supports and deities: God alone creates and governs, and people must thank and worship Him alone because they return to Him for judgment.
rows.anchor: the one and only God is the sole creator and administrator of this universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter is certain; wrongdoers will confess and ask to return to earthly life for faith and good deeds, but their pleas will not be accepted.
rows.anchor: the wrongdoers will confess their crimes and request God to give them a chance to go back into the previous world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage first discusses monotheism in this verse and the next few, then turns to the Hereafter and its events.
rows.anchor: In the verse under discussion and in the next few ones, monotheism is discussed. After this, the Hereafter and what will befall there is discussed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six days are six phases because a divine day equals a thousand human years.
rows.anchor: the days referred to are the days of God and it is clarified further down that a day of God equals one thousand human years.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gradual, elaborate creation of the heavens, earth, and what lies between shows that the world is purposeful and wise, not made for amusement.
rows.anchor: This gradual and elaborate manner evidences the fact that this world has a purpose and wisdom behind it: it has not been made for entertainment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s ascending the throne means He continued directly governing the world after creating it; this refutes the idolaters’ idea that He delegated control to favored beings and withdrew.
rows.anchor: He consigned its management and control to some favoured ones and Himself became aloof to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God directly controls everything, all will be gathered before Him for judgment, and no one can support or intercede for another against Him.
rows.anchor: You have no guardian or intercessor besides Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse denies any guardian or intercessor besides God.
rows.anchor: You have no guardian or intercessor besides Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the warning’s consequences rest on facts the audience acknowledges, the verse rebukes them for failing to heed these clear matters.
rows.anchor: Will you not take heed?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All affairs from heaven to earth are under God’s control.
rows.anchor: The verse states that all affairs of this world from the heavens to the earth are under God’s control.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This refutes idolaters’ notion that God governs heaven but delegates the distant earth to agents; the Qur’an elsewhere challenges the idea of separate gods for heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: This is actually a refutation of a false notion of the Idolaters that the earth is a far off area of this universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “to Him it returns” means “to refer.”
rows.anchor: here means “to refer.” The implication is that after giving the directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affairs first issue from God and are then referred back to Him; He is not aloof and knows whether His agents have carried out their duties and how.
rows.anchor: everything is presented back to Him and He is fully aware if His workers and the implementers of His will have discharged their duties

rows.speaker: People generally
rows.claim: People commonly take the thousand-year day to mean Judgment Day, when deeds are presented, and treat its duration as a metaphor for that day’s severity; Islahi rejects this reading.
rows.anchor: People have generally considered the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an 22:47 answers people who demand prompt punishment: a divine day equals a thousand human years, so people should not measure God’s plans by their shorter timescale.
rows.anchor: This verse has come in response to the people’s claim to hasten the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What seems a long delay to people may amount to barely a second by God’s measure of time.
rows.anchor: The fact is that as per the measure of God maybe even a second might not have elapsed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse means that all planning belongs to God: directives issue from Him and return to Him according to His timescale, whose consequences and wisdom people cannot fully grasp.
rows.anchor: all planning is in the hands of God. Directives originate from Him and then return to Him as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should be patient and wait for God’s plans to unfold instead of hastening them.
rows.anchor: they should not show haste in the matters of God. In fact, they should show patience and wait for them to materialize.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God, both mighty and merciful, knows the seen and unseen and all the universe’s secrets; people should trust Him.
rows.anchor: it is only the powerful and merciful God Who is aware of the known and the unknown.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi anticipates a possible conflict between the thousand-year day here and the fifty-thousand-year day in Sūrah al-Maʿārij.
rows.anchor: It is possible that a question arise in the mind of someone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The different durations may reflect differences among the orbits, since planets and stars have days of different lengths.
rows.anchor: This difference is based on difference between the size of the orbits. For this reason, various planets and stars have days of different duration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thousand-year verse concerns affairs being presented to God, whereas al-Maʿārij describes angels and Gabriel appearing directly before Him.
rows.anchor: presenting of matters before God is under discussion while in Sūrah al-Ma‘ārij, the direct appearance of the angels and Gabriel before God is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is possible that affairs are presented in a day of a thousand earth years while angels appear directly in one of fifty thousand; these are matters of the unseen, but the verses do not contradict.
rows.anchor: These matters relate to the realm of the unknown (ghayb). Nothing can be said about them with certainty. However, this much is evident that there is no contradiction between the two verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge of the seen and unseen and His power and mercy prepare the reader for the warning about the Hereafter that follows.
rows.anchor: The attributes of God mentioned in the previous verse – as the one who is aware of the seen and the unseen and who is powerful and merciful – serve to form a prelude to sounding a warning about the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation testifies to God’s power, wisdom, providence, and knowledge; reflecting even on the smallest created thing amazes a person and evokes praise of God as the best creator.
rows.anchor: whatever He has created bears testimony to His power, wisdom, providence and profound knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wise Creator would not make the universe purposeless; there must be a day to distinguish truth from falsehood and reward the grateful while punishing the heedless.
rows.anchor: it is essential that a day come in which he distinguishes between truth and falsehood and then reward those who

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those punished are people who lived carelessly, ignored God’s wisdom, and gave no weight to people who reflected on it.
rows.anchor: These latter type of people were the ones who neither deliberated on the wisdom of God nor gave importance to others who deliberated on it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human creation from clay demonstrates God’s power, wisdom, and providence: the conceited person can reflect on how God transformed clay into a majestic human being.
rows.anchor: he was created from clay. His structure was fashioned from clay and from this clay signs of life appeared in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human progeny is brought forth in a second phase from the essence of a lowly, impure fluid.
rows.anchor: in this phase his progeny came into being through the essence of a trivial and impure fluid instead of being created from clay.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word sawwā means to perfect something and give it its finishing touches.
rows.anchor: The word ةیتسو means to perfect something and give it its final touches

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the third phase God finished the clay-made human, breathed His spirit into him, and gave him sight, hearing, and cognition that distinguish him from other life forms.
rows.anchor: he gave finishing touches to this man made of clay and breathed His spirit into Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine spirit is a divine spark that makes human perception and cognition radiant, which is why the human is called the best of creation.
rows.anchor: With this divine spirit, a person also has a divine spark in him and it is as a result of this divine spark that his sight, hearing and cognition became so radiant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without that radiance a person’s inner self becomes dark like an animal’s; animals have eyes, ears, and hearts but lack the divine spark and its human capacities.
rows.anchor: Beasts also have eyes, ears and hearts; however, they are deprived of the divine spark.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s will and intention can sustain, increase, or diminish this divine spark.
rows.anchor: it falls under man’s will and intention to sustain, increase or decrease this spark.
